entries.lesson_title: System Output from Input and Impulse Response
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the LTI system output by evaluating the continuous-time convolution integral for a given input signal and impulse response.

sections.section_title: Introduction to System Output from Input and Impulse Response
sections.learning_goal: Connect an LTI system's input, impulse response, and output through the continuous-time convolution formula.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State explicitly that an LTI system output is computed by convolving the input signal with the impulse response.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A system with named input x(t), named impulse response h(t), and output y(t) written as y(t)=(x*h)(t).
paragraph_plan: Identify x(t) as the input signal, h(t) as the impulse response, and y(t) as the output signal.
State that for an LTI system, knowing x(t) and h(t) is enough to compute the output by convolution.
Introduce the convolution relation y(t)=(x*h)(t) and emphasize that t is the output time.
Introduce the dummy integration variable tau and explain that x(t) becomes x(tau) while h(t) becomes h(t-tau).
Preview the lesson flow: identify the roles, write the integral, substitute the functions, and evaluate the resulting integral.
display_math_plan: y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening short and directive: no derivation of convolution, no region-finding, and no graphical overlap work.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Input, Impulse Response, and Output
sections.learning_goal: Identify x(t), h(t), and y(t) from a direct LTI convolution problem statement before setting up the integral.

question_policy.answer_format: one selected statement correctly matching the input, impulse response, and output notation
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has input x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3) and impulse response h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t). Which statement correctly identifies x(t), h(t), and y(t)?
distractor_plan: Swap the input and impulse response labels.
Treat h(t-tau) as the original impulse response instead of the shifted form used inside convolution.
Label the output as x(t)*h(t) without naming y(t).
Mistake the system rule or integral expression for one of the given signals.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A causal LTI system is driven by input x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2) and has impulse response h(t)=e^{-t}u(t). Identify the input signal, impulse response, and output symbol.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Label x(t) as the input, h(t) as the impulse response, and y(t)=(x*h)(t) as the output to be computed.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active task after the tutorial; it requires role recognition only, not integral setup or evaluation.
solution_step_plan: Read the statement and locate the phrase naming the input.
Read the statement and locate the phrase naming the impulse response.
Name the unknown output as y(t).
Connect the output notation to y(t)=(x*h)(t) without performing the convolution.
practice_variation_axes: Change the input signal expression.
Change the impulse response expression.
Vary whether the problem says output, response, or system output.
Use step, pulse, or one-sided exponential expressions already aligned with the course map.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section as a notation-control step so later sections can rely on stable meanings for x(t), h(t), and y(t).

sections.section_title: Writing the Output as a Convolution Integral
sections.learning_goal: Write the LTI output y(t) as the convolution integral of x(tau) with h(t-tau).

question_policy.answer_format: a convolution integral for y(t) using x(tau), h(t-tau), infinite bounds, and d tau
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has input x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1) and impulse response h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t). Write y(t) as a convolution integral before substituting the formulas.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An LTI system has input x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1) and impulse response h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t). Write the output y(t) as a convolution integral before substituting the formulas.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau and leave the given signal formulas for the next substitution step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends role identification into the standard convolution-integral form while still delaying substitution and evaluation.
solution_step_plan: Identify x(t) and h(t) from the statement.
Start with y(t)=(x*h)(t).
Change the input argument from t to tau.
Change the impulse-response argument from t to t-tau.
Write the integral over tau with d tau and infinite bounds.
practice_variation_axes: Change the specific input and impulse response expressions.
Use different decay rates in exponential examples.
Use rectangular pulses or unit-step-windowed signals without asking for bounds yet.
Vary whether the prompt says output y(t) or system output.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not substitute x(tau) or h(t-tau) in this section; the target move is forming the convolution template from the identified roles.

sections.section_title: Substituting x(tau) and h(t - tau) into the Integral
sections.learning_goal: Substitute the given input and impulse-response formulas into x(tau) and h(t-tau) inside the convolution integral.

question_policy.answer_format: a convolution integral with x(tau) and h(t-tau) replaced by the corresponding formulas
question_policy.practice_question_model: For x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1) and h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t), write the substituted convolution integral for y(t), but do not evaluate it.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1) and h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t), substitute x(tau) and h(t-tau) into the convolution integral for y(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Rewrite the integrand as [u(tau)-u(tau-1)]e^{-2(t-tau)}u(t-tau) inside the convolution integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the integral form from the previous section but adds the argument changes needed to insert the actual signal formulas.
solution_step_plan: Start from y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
Rewrite x(t) as x(tau) by replacing every t in the input formula with tau.
Rewrite h(t) as h(t-tau) by replacing every t in the impulse-response formula with t-tau.
Multiply the substituted factors inside the integrand.
Stop before simplifying bounds or evaluating the integral.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse width in the input.
Change the exponential decay constant in the impulse response.
Swap in a one-sided exponential input with a step-like impulse response.
Vary how many occurrences of the argument t must be replaced.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize argument substitution and defer overlap bounds or region splitting; this lesson section should not become a full piecewise-convolution lesson.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Integral for the Output Signal
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate a prepared convolution integral to obtain the output expression for y(t) on a stated time region.

question_policy.answer_format: a simplified output expression y(t) for the stated time region
question_policy.practice_question_model: For an LTI system with input x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t) and impulse response h(t)=u(t), the convolution setup on 0<t<1 is y(t)=\int_0^t e^{-2\tau}\,d\tau. Evaluate y(t) on this interval.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For an LTI system with input x(t)=e^{-t}u(t) and impulse response h(t)=u(t), the convolution setup on 0<t<1 is y(t)=\int_0^t e^{-\tau}\,d\tau. Evaluate y(t) on this interval.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute the definite integral and report the output as y(t)=1-e^{-t} for 0<t<1.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the final procedural step: after roles, integral form, and substitution are already controlled, the learner now evaluates the prepared integral.
solution_step_plan: Confirm the integral and the stated time region.
Find an antiderivative of the integrand with respect to tau.
Apply the upper and lower bounds.
Simplify the resulting expression.
Attach the stated time region to the output expression.
practice_variation_axes: Change the exponential decay constant.
Change the upper bound from t to a simple stated bound when appropriate.
Use simple polynomial or constant integrands only when the resulting integral stays focused on convolution output.
Keep the time region stated so practice does not require discovering piecewise regions.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the evaluation algebra simple enough that the learning target remains direct convolution output, not integration technique or time-region partitioning.

entries.lesson_core_move: Partition a direct convolution calculation into time regions by tracking how the overlap between x(tau) and h(t - tau) changes as t moves.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Breaking Convolution into Time Regions
sections.learning_goal: Explain why a direct convolution calculation is split at the t-values where the overlap pattern between fixed x(\tau) and moving h(t - \tau) changes.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show a tau-axis with the fixed support of x(\tau) and several positions of the moving support of h(t - \tau), labeled before contact, partial overlap, and after separation, with endpoint contact times marked on the t-axis.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a clean support-interval diagram rather than detailed signal amplitudes; the visual should reduce load by making the changing overlap pattern visible.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that the convolution integral has different integration bounds in different t-regions because the support overlap between x(\tau) and h(t - \tau) changes as t changes.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use one finite support interval for x(\tau) and one finite support interval for h(t - \tau), with all endpoints visible on a single tau-axis.
paragraph_plan: Start from the convolution integral and state that only tau-values where both factors are nonzero can contribute.
Identify x(\tau) as the fixed support constraint and h(t - \tau) as the support interval that moves as t changes.
Define contact times as t-values where an endpoint of h(t - \tau) lines up with an endpoint of x(\tau).
Explain that the open intervals between consecutive contact times are the time regions, because the overlap pattern stays the same inside each one.
Preview that later examples will find contact times, order them, classify overlap regions, and assign integration bounds.
display_math_plan: y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau
x(\tau)\neq 0 \text{ on } [a,b]
h(t-\tau)\neq 0 \text{ on } [t-d,t-c]
\text{overlap in }\tau=[a,b]\cap[t-d,t-c]

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial conceptual and procedural; do not evaluate any convolution integral or introduce amplitude-specific calculations.

sections.section_title: Finding Contact Times Between x(tau) and h(t - tau)
sections.learning_goal: Find the t-values where endpoints of the fixed support of x(\tau) align with endpoints of the moving support of h(t - \tau).

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the fixed support of x(\tau) on [0,3] and the moving support of h(t - \tau) on [t-2,t] on a tau-axis, with endpoints labeled so endpoint-alignment equations can be read from the diagram.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Generate section and question visuals as support diagrams with labeled endpoints; avoid using amplitude shape as the source of the task unless it is needed only to show nonzero support.

question_policy.answer_format: A sorted list of contact times, such as t=0,2,3,5.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a diagram where x(\tau) is nonzero on [1,4] and h(t-\tau) is nonzero on [t-3,t-1], find all t-values when an endpoint of h(t-\tau) aligns with an endpoint of x(\tau).
distractor_plan: Omit the interior endpoint alignments and give only first and last contact times.
Reverse the signs when solving equations involving t-shifted endpoints.
Report tau endpoint values instead of the corresponding t-values.
Include repeated or unsorted breakpoint values without simplifying the list.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(\tau) nonzero on 0\le \tau\le 3 and h(t-\tau) nonzero on t-2\le \tau\le t, find the contact times between their support endpoints.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Collect every t-value where a moving support endpoint lines up with a fixed support endpoint.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the tutorial's qualitative idea of changing overlap to the exact endpoint equations that create breakpoints.
solution_step_plan: Name the fixed endpoints 0 and 3 for x(\tau).
Name the moving endpoints t-2 and t for h(t-\tau).
Set each moving endpoint equal to each fixed endpoint.
Solve the four endpoint-alignment equations for t.
Sort the resulting t-values and label them as contact times.
practice_variation_axes: fixed support endpoints
width of the moving support interval
offset in the moving support endpoints
integer versus fractional contact times

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the work focused on endpoint alignment; do not classify regions or assign integration bounds in this section.

sections.section_title: Ordering Breakpoints on the t-Axis
sections.learning_goal: Place all contact times in increasing order on the t-axis so they define the candidate time regions for the convolution.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the support intervals that generate several unsorted contact times, plus a blank t-axis underneath where the breakpoints should be ordered from left to right.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the image to connect endpoint contacts to a t-axis partition; the final ordered list should still be represented symbolically.

question_policy.answer_format: An increasing ordered list of breakpoints followed by the induced open t-intervals.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For contact times t=5, t=-1, t=2, and t=0, order the breakpoints on the t-axis and list the open intervals they create.
distractor_plan: List breakpoints in the order they were found rather than increasing t-order.
Drop negative or fractional breakpoint values while sorting.
Create intervals using closed endpoints instead of open regions between breakpoints.
Forget the two exterior regions before the first breakpoint and after the last breakpoint.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(\tau) nonzero on -1\le \tau\le 2 and h(t-\tau) nonzero on t-3\le \tau\le t-1, find the contact times and order the resulting breakpoints on the t-axis.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Turn endpoint-alignment times into a left-to-right t-axis partition.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the need to organize contact times as a t-axis partition instead of just collecting them.
solution_step_plan: Write the fixed endpoints and moving endpoints.
Solve the endpoint-alignment equations to obtain candidate breakpoints.
Remove duplicate breakpoint values if they occur.
Sort the breakpoints from smallest to largest.
List the t-regions determined by the ordered breakpoints, including the exterior intervals.
practice_variation_axes: number of distinct breakpoints
presence of negative breakpoints
presence of duplicate endpoint alignments
fractional endpoint values

sections.handoff_notes: The worked solution should emphasize ordering and interval creation, not the later decision about whether each interval has overlap.

sections.section_title: Classifying No-Overlap and Overlap Regions
sections.learning_goal: Classify t-regions by whether the fixed x(\tau) support and the moving h(t - \tau) support overlap inside that region.

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show representative positions of h(t - \tau) for each ordered t-region relative to a fixed x(\tau) support, with visual overlap shaded only where both supports cover the same tau-values.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use small multiples or stacked support lines so the learner can compare one representative t-value from each region without tracking a moving animation.

question_policy.answer_format: One label selected from: no-overlap, overlap.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For x(\tau) supported on [0,4] and h(t-\tau) supported on [t-2,t], classify the region 1<t<2 as no-overlap or overlap.
distractor_plan: Treat endpoint contact as an entire overlap interval.
Classify a region using a boundary value instead of an interior representative t-value.
Confuse overlap in tau with positive t-values.
Ignore one support interval and classify from only the position of h(t-\tau).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Using the ordered breakpoints t=0,2,3,5 for x(\tau) supported on [0,3] and h(t-\tau) supported on [t-2,t], classify each resulting t-region as no-overlap or overlap.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Decide which t-regions produce a nonempty tau-overlap and which produce zero contribution.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the ordered t-axis partition to attach a qualitative overlap status to each region.
solution_step_plan: List the regions determined by the ordered breakpoints.
Choose one representative t-value from each region.
Substitute that t-value into the moving support endpoints.
Compare the moving support interval with the fixed x(\tau) interval.
Label the region as no-overlap when the intersection is empty and overlap when it is nonempty.
practice_variation_axes: which t-region is queried
whether the queried region is exterior or interior
support widths
boundary values that create endpoint-only contact

sections.handoff_notes: Questions should check region classification, not ask for integration bounds yet; endpoint-only contact should be treated as a boundary between regions, not a positive-width overlap region.

sections.section_title: Assigning Integration Bounds for Each Time Region
sections.learning_goal: Write the tau integration bounds for each overlap time region by intersecting the fixed support of x(\tau) with the moving support of h(t - \tau).

image_policy.image_description_seed: Show the fixed x(\tau) support and moving h(t - \tau) support for each overlap t-region, with the lower and upper tau bounds highlighted as the endpoints of the shaded intersection.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use the visual to show why the bound is a fixed endpoint in some regions and a t-dependent endpoint in others; do not include integral evaluation.

question_policy.answer_format: A piecewise list or table giving tau lower and upper bounds for each overlap t-region.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For x(\tau) supported on [0,3] and h(t-\tau) supported on [t-2,t], give the tau integration bounds for each overlap region 0<t<2, 2<t<3, and 3<t<5.
distractor_plan: Use the full support of x(\tau) as the bounds in every overlap region.
Use the full support of h(t-\tau) as the bounds in every overlap region.
Swap lower and upper bounds when a t-dependent endpoint is involved.
Assign bounds to no-overlap exterior regions instead of marking them as zero contribution.
Evaluate the convolution integral instead of stopping at the bounds.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For x(\tau) supported on [0,3] and h(t-\tau) supported on [t-2,t], assign the tau integration bounds for each overlap time region.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce the correct lower and upper tau bounds for every nonzero time region without evaluating the integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Converts overlap classification into the exact tau bounds needed for the later direct convolution calculation.
solution_step_plan: Start from the ordered breakpoints and keep only regions with nonempty overlap.
Write the overlap interval as [0,3]\cap[t-2,t].
For each overlap region, determine which endpoint is the larger lower bound.
For each overlap region, determine which endpoint is the smaller upper bound.
Record the bounds as a piecewise table matched to the corresponding t-regions.
practice_variation_axes: fixed support interval
moving support interval
number of overlap regions
which bounds are fixed versus t-dependent
whether no-overlap regions must be excluded

sections.handoff_notes: This is the capstone section for the lesson; stop after setting bounds so the following lesson can perform direct convolution computations.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the convolution of finite-duration input and impulse-response signals by finding overlap intervals, setting integration bounds, and assembling the piecewise LTI output.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution with Finite-Duration Signals
sections.learning_goal: Explain the direct finite-duration convolution workflow: use supports to find output support, split time into overlap regions, set tau bounds, evaluate each piece, and assemble y(t).

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; use support intervals, inequalities, and piecewise notation as the working objects.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that finite-duration convolution becomes manageable when the infinite convolution integral is replaced by region-specific integrals over the overlap of x(\tau) and h(t-\tau).
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use two constant finite-duration signals, such as x(t)=1 on 0<=t<=3 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=2, with both signals zero outside their intervals.
paragraph_plan: Start from the LTI output formula y(t)=(x*h)(t) and the convolution integral over tau.
State that finite-duration signals are zero outside bounded support intervals, so most tau-values contribute nothing.
Explain that x(\tau) gives a fixed tau-support while h(t-\tau) gives a t-dependent tau-support.
Show that each time region has its own overlap interval, which becomes the integration bounds for that piece of y(t).
Preview the lesson progression: output support, partial-overlap bounds, full-overlap bounds, piece evaluation, and final piecewise assembly.
display_math_plan: y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau
x(\tau)\neq 0 \text{ on } [a,b]
h(t-\tau)\neq 0 \text{ when } t-\tau \in [c,d]
\tau \in [a,b]\cap[t-d,t-c]
\operatorname{supp}(x*h)\subseteq [a+c,b+d]

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as a compact workflow introduction. Do not compute a full convolution yet; establish the support-overlap-to-bounds-to-piecewise-output chain.

sections.section_title: Finding the Output Support from Finite-Duration Signal Supports
sections.learning_goal: Find the possible nonzero support of y(t)=x*h by adding the earliest and latest support endpoints of the two finite-duration signals.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; endpoint addition and interval notation are sufficient.

question_policy.answer_format: An interval for the possible nonzero support of y(t), such as [1,7].
question_policy.practice_question_model: If x(t) is nonzero only on -1<=t<=2 and h(t) is nonzero only on 0<=t<=3, find the possible nonzero support of y(t)=(x*h)(t).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Suppose x(t) is nonzero only on 0<=t<=3 and h(t) is nonzero only on 1<=t<=4. Find the possible nonzero support of y(t)=(x*h)(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify that y(t) can be nonzero only for 1<=t<=7.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Turns the tutorial's support idea into the first concrete calculation by finding the outer time interval before any integration bounds are set.
solution_step_plan: Name the support of x(t) as [0,3].
Name the support of h(t) as [1,4].
Add the left endpoints to find the first possible contact time.
Add the right endpoints to find the last possible separation time.
State the possible output support as the interval between those two times.
practice_variation_axes: Change the support endpoints of x(t).
Change the support endpoints of h(t).
Include negative support endpoints.
Use closed interval notation or inequality notation for the answer.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not ask for overlap bounds or output formulas in this section. The target is only the outer support interval for y(t).

sections.section_title: Setting Integral Bounds in a Partial-Overlap Region
sections.learning_goal: Set tau integration bounds for a rising partial-overlap region by intersecting the fixed support of x(\tau) with the moving support of h(t-\tau).

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the bounds should be derived from symbolic support inequalities.

question_policy.answer_format: A bounded integral setup or tau interval for the stated partial-overlap t-region.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let x(t)=1 on 0<=t<=4 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=1, with both zero otherwise. For 0<t<1, set the tau bounds for y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let x(t)=1 on 0<=t<=3 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=2, with both signals zero otherwise. For 0<t<2, set the tau integration bounds for y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive the partial-overlap bounds 0<=\tau<=t for 0<t<2.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the outer output support to the first nonzero region, where the overlap grows from zero and one bound depends on t.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite the fixed support as x(\tau) nonzero on 0<=\tau<=3.
Convert h(t-\tau) nonzero on 0<=t-\tau<=2 into t-2<=\tau<=t.
Intersect [0,3] with [t-2,t].
Use the condition 0<t<2 to decide that the lower bound is 0 and the upper bound is t.
Write the bounded integral over 0<=\tau<=t without evaluating it.
practice_variation_axes: Change the width of h(t).
Change the fixed support length of x(t).
Ask for the first partial-overlap region after initial contact.
Use constant amplitudes that should not affect the bounds.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section focused on bounds only. The example writer may show the integrand, but should not evaluate the integral.

sections.section_title: Setting Integral Bounds in a Full-Overlap Region
sections.learning_goal: Set tau integration bounds for a full-overlap region where the shorter shifted support lies entirely inside the longer fixed support.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the full-overlap bounds follow from symbolic endpoint comparison.

question_policy.answer_format: A bounded integral setup or tau interval for the stated full-overlap t-region.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Let x(t)=1 on 0<=t<=5 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=2, with both zero otherwise. For 2<t<5, set the tau bounds for y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let x(t)=1 on 0<=t<=3 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=2, with both signals zero otherwise. For 2<t<3, set the tau integration bounds for y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive the full-overlap bounds t-2<=\tau<=t for 2<t<3.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same signals but moves to the middle region, where both integration bounds come from the shifted h(t-\tau) support.
solution_step_plan: Start from the same support intersection [0,3]\cap[t-2,t].
Use the condition 2<t<3 to compare t-2 with 0.
Use the condition 2<t<3 to compare t with 3.
Conclude that [t-2,t] is fully inside [0,3] in this region.
Write the bounded integral over t-2<=\tau<=t without evaluating it.
practice_variation_axes: Change the length of the fixed support.
Change the length of the moving support.
Use a different full-overlap region where both bounds are t-dependent.
Keep amplitudes simple so endpoint comparison remains the target.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the contrast with the previous partial-overlap section explicit: here the moving support supplies both bounds.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Finite-Duration Convolution Pieces
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate bounded convolution integrals on stated finite-duration time regions while keeping each formula attached to its own region.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the work is definite integration over already-determined bounds.

question_policy.answer_format: One or more evaluated y(t) expressions matched to the stated time regions.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For x(t)=3 on 0<=t<=4 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=1, evaluate y(t) on the regions 0<t<1 with bounds 0<=\tau<=t and 1<t<4 with bounds t-1<=\tau<=t.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let x(t)=2 on 0<=t<=3 and h(t)=1 on 0<=t<=2, with both signals zero otherwise. Evaluate y(t) on the regions 0<t<2 with bounds 0<=\tau<=t and 2<t<3 with bounds t-2<=\tau<=t.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute the two region formulas y(t)=2t for 0<t<2 and y(t)=4 for 2<t<3.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the bounds from the partial-overlap and full-overlap cases, then adds the integration step needed to produce output formulas.
solution_step_plan: Substitute the constant values of x(\tau) and h(t-\tau) into the integrand on the stated regions.
Evaluate the integral over 0<=\tau<=t for the partial-overlap region.
Evaluate the integral over t-2<=\tau<=t for the full-overlap region.
Simplify each result.
Attach each result to the time region that produced it.
practice_variation_axes: Change the constant amplitude of x(t).
Change the constant amplitude of h(t).
Ask for one region or two adjacent regions.
Use bounds that are already supplied so the section tests evaluation rather than region discovery.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not require the full piecewise output yet. The writer should emphasize evaluating prepared pieces and preserving their region labels.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Finite-Duration Output
sections.learning_goal: Assemble the zero regions and evaluated nonzero pieces into a complete piecewise expression for the finite-duration convolution output y(t).

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the final handoff should be a symbolic piecewise function.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Checking Continuity of a Convolution Result
sections.learning_goal: Introduce continuity checking as a symbolic verification step for piecewise convolution results by comparing adjacent boundary values before interpreting the result as an LTI output.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that a piecewise convolution result should be checked at each shared time-region boundary by evaluating the formula from the left and the formula from the right at the boundary.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a two-piece result with y(t) = 0 for t < a and y(t) = t - a for a <= t < b, so both sides give 0 at t = a.
paragraph_plan: Start from the fact that direct convolution often produces a piecewise output because the overlap changes from one time region to the next.
Define a continuity check as evaluating the adjacent formulas at the same boundary time and comparing the left-hand and right-hand values.
Explain that matching values pass the check, while a mismatch is an error flag for algebra, integration bounds, or region assignment.
Show the simplest zero-to-nonzero boundary symbolically, with the zero piece and the first nonzero piece both evaluated at the boundary.
Preview the progression: first check an outer boundary, then an interior boundary, then all boundaries, then use a failed check to locate a likely error.
display_math_plan: Display the general boundary condition: value from the left piece at t = a should equal value from the right piece at t = a.
Display the base-case check: left value = 0 and right value = a - a = 0.
Display the diagnostic conclusion: matching boundary values pass; nonmatching boundary values flag a likely local error.
